name: ryu (Ryū float-to-string)
verdict_reason: The README's approximately 2-5x claim holds at its low end: dtoa-benchmark on Rust 1.97.0 measures 31.1 vs 68.8 ns per f64 (2.21x) on a Threadripper 9975WX and 26.9 vs 63.9 ns (2.38x) on an M4 Max. It is no longer the fastest option: zmij is 3.7x faster in the same table and replaced ryu inside serde_json.
tier_reason: Public benchmark with CPUs, Rust 1.97.0 and -C target-cpu=native stated; maintained by ryu's author.
claimed_speedup: README: approximately 2-5x faster than std. dtoa-benchmark: 31.1 vs 68.8 ns per f64 (2.21x) on Threadripper 9975WX, 26.9 vs 63.9 ns (2.38x) on M4 Max; zmij 8.5 ns and 5.9 ns on the same machines.
workload: Random f64 bit patterns truncated to 1-17 significant digits; fastest pass per precision group, averaged across groups.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 9975WX; Apple M4 Max
one_liner: Ryū shortest float-to-string: 2.2x-2.4x faster than std's float Display, now overtaken by zmij.
how_it_is_fast: Ryū (Ulf Adams, PLDI 2018) finds the shortest decimal that round-trips using precomputed power-of-5 tables and 128-bit multiplies, with no big-integer fallback, and writes into a stack buffer instead of through Formatter.
use_it_when: Existing code on ryu that cannot take a new dependency
You want the Ryū algorithm's published correctness proof
skip_it_when: New code: zmij is 3.7x faster in the same benchmark and serde_json moved to it in 1.0.147
You need std's exact output; ryu writes 1.23e40 where std writes the full digits
caveats: The README's own Rust-vs-std numbers are chart-only; the text numbers come from dtoa-benchmark
std's Display never uses exponent notation, so it writes longer strings for extreme values
tradeoffs: Output format differs from std for large and small magnitudes

evidence.quote: The benchmark shows Ryū approximately 2-5x faster than the standard library across a range of f32 and f64 inputs.
